api/Unravel.Core.AutoStaticsCleanupAttri.summary: Class AutoStaticsCleanupAttribute Namespace Unravel.Core Marks a class whose static state must be reset when a script domain is unloaded (CoreCLR backend). On Mono, unloading a domain destroys its statics wholesale. On CoreCLR a collectible AssemblyLoadContext only unloads once nothing references it anymore, so static caches in a surviving assembly (e.g. managers holding script instances or script Type objects) would silently keep the unloaded domain alive. The runtime processes this attribute right before any domain is unloaded: If the class defines static void OnStaticsCleanup() (any visibility), that method is invoked and nothing else happens - use it to re-create managers or clear collections selectively. Otherwise every non-readonly static field is reset to its default value. Readonly statics cannot be cleared by reflection and produce a warning - define OnStaticsCleanup for those. The attribute is matched by name, so any assembly may use it without referencing the engine. On Mono it is ignored. api/Unravel.Core.ForceMode.html.title: Enum ForceMode | Unravel Engine Scripting API
api/Unravel.Core.ForceMode.html.summary: Enum ForceMode Namespace Unravel.Core Specifies how forces are applied to physics components. public enum ForceMode : byte Fields Acceleration = 1 Add a continuous acceleration to the rigidbody, ignoring its mass. Apply the acceleration in each FixedUpdate over a duration of time. In contrast to Force, Acceleration will move every rigidbody the same way regardless of differences in mass. This mode is useful if you just want to control the acceleration of an object directly. In this mode, the unit of the force parameter is applied to the rigidbody as distance / time^2. Force = 0 Add a continuous force to the rigidbody, using its mass. Apply the force in each FixedUpdate over a duration of time. This mode depends on the mass of the rigidbody, so more force must be applied to push or twist higher-mass objects the same amount as lower-mass objects. This mode is useful for setting up realistic physics where it takes more force to move heavier objects. In this mode, the unit of the force parameter is applied to the rigidbody as mass * distance / time^2. Impulse = 2 Add an instant force impulse to the rigidbody, using its mass. Apply the impulse force instantly with a single function call. This mode depends on the mass of the rigidbody, so more force must be applied to push or twist higher-mass objects the same amount as lower-mass objects. This mode is useful for applying forces that happen instantly, such as forces from explosions or collisions. In this mode, the unit of the force parameter is applied to the rigidbody as mass * distance / time. VelocityChange = 3 Add an instant velocity change to the rigidbody, ignoring its mass. Apply the velocity change instantly with a single function call. In contrast to Impulse, VelocityChange will change the velocity of every rigidbody the same way regardless of differences in mass. This mode is useful for something like a fleet of differently-sized spaceships that you want to control without accounting for differences in mass. In this mode, the unit of the force parameter is applied to the rigidbody as distance / time.

api/Unravel.Core.IK.html.summary: Class IK Namespace Unravel.Core Inverse-kinematics helpers for skeletal chains. Call these from OnUpdate. Scripts run after the animation system has evaluated the pose and before skinning, so bone writes made there are what gets rendered. Writing bones from OnFixedUpdate does not work - animation will overwrite them later in the frame. Every method returns true when a pose was written. A false means the chain was too short, the goal was not finite, or the weight was zero - not that the target was out of reach (an unreachable target still produces a valid stretched pose). The position solvers only orient the bones that drive the chain, never the end effector itself, so a solved foot keeps the orientation animation gave it. Follow a position solve with SetIKRotation(Entity, Quaternion, float) to pin a foot to a slope or keep an aimed hand level. Poles must come from a reference the solve does not move - the character root, or a dedicated hint entity. A pole derived from the end effector's own transform closes a feedback loop: the solve rotates the effector, the pole follows it, the chain chases the pole, and the limb spins. public static class IK Inheritance object IK Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Methods GetBoneAxis(Entity) Bone-local direction from entity toward its first child, i.e. the axis the bone visually runs ALONG. Returns Vector3.forward for leaf bones. Use this with SetIKAim(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, float, float) only when you want to point the bone itself at something - a barrel, a tentacle, a limb. It is the wrong axis for a "face the target" aim on a spine, chest or head: aiming a spine along its own length points the torso at the target and folds the character in half. Which axis represents a bone's FACING cannot be derived from the skeleton (that is what a humanoid avatar mapping is for), so pass it explicitly - Vector3.forward for most rigs. public static Vector3 GetBoneAxis(Entity entity) Parameters entity Entity Returns Vector3 GetFacingAxis(Entity, Vector3) Bone-local axis of entity that currently points along worldDirection, snapped to the nearest signed unit axis. This is how you get the forwardAxis for SetIKAim(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, float, float) on a torso or head without guessing. A rig authored with the chest's local -Z out of the front is structurally identical to one with +Z out of the front, and importers do not normalise it - so ask the rig which local axis lines up with the character's forward: spineAimAxis = IK.GetFacingAxis(Spine, transform.forward); Sample it in a neutral pose (OnStart is fine). Snapping means a spine slightly bent by the current animation frame still resolves cleanly. Contrast with GetBoneAxis(Entity), which returns the axis the bone runs ALONG - a different question with a different answer. public static Vector3 GetFacingAxis(Entity entity, Vector3 worldDirection) Parameters entity Entity worldDirection Vector3 Returns Vector3 SetIKAim(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, float, float) Points a bone-local axis at target. Imported rigs rarely run their bones along +Z - Mixamo bones run along local +Y - so pass the rig's actual axis, or GetBoneAxis(Entity) to derive it from the skeleton. public static bool SetIKAim(Entity entity, Vector3 target, Vector3 forwardAxis, Vector3 upAxis, Vector3 worldUp, float maxAngleDegrees = 0, float weight = 1) Parameters entity Entity target Vector3 forwardAxis Vector3 Bone-local axis that ends up pointing at the target. upAxis Vector3 Bone-local axis kept close to worldUp. worldUp Vector3 World-space up reference. Pass Vector3.zero to keep the bone's existing twist instead of forcing a roll - the safer default for spines. maxAngleDegrees float Cone limit measured from the bone's current forward. 0 leaves the aim unlimited. The swing is clamped to the cone, so the bone eases to a stop at the limit rather than the caller having to switch the solve off. weight float Returns bool SetIKLookAtPosition(Entity, Vector3, float) Orients entity so its local +Z axis points at target, blended by weight and preserving the bone's twist. Matches the engine's entity convention; for skeleton bones prefer SetIKAim(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, float, float). public static bool SetIKLookAtPosition(Entity entity, Vector3 target, float weight = 1) Parameters entity Entity target Vector3 weight float Returns bool SetIKPositionCCD(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, int, int, float, float) Solves a CCD IK chain so the end effector reaches target. pole is a world-space hint for which side of the (root -> end) line intermediate joints should bend toward - typically a point in front of the character at knee height for legs. Pass Vector3.zero to disable the constraint. public static bool SetIKPositionCCD(Entity entity, Vector3 target, Vector3 pole, int numBonesInChain, int maxIterations = 20, float threshold = 0.001, float weight = 1) Parameters entity Entity target Vector3 pole Vector3 numBonesInChain int maxIterations int threshold float weight float Blend against the animated pose, 0..1. Returns bool SetIKPositionFabrik(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, int, int, float, float) Solves a FABRIK IK chain so the end effector reaches target. pole is a world-space hint for which side of the (root -> end) line intermediate joints should bend toward. Without a pole, FABRIK may pick any geometrically valid bend direction - which on steep slopes causes knees to collapse inward. Pass Vector3.zero to disable the constraint. public static bool SetIKPositionFabrik(Entity entity, Vector3 target, Vector3 pole, int numBonesInChain, int maxIterations = 20, float threshold = 0.001, float weight = 1) Parameters entity Entity target Vector3 pole Vector3 numBonesInChain int maxIterations int threshold float weight float Blend against the animated pose, 0..1. Returns bool SetIKPositionTwoBone(Entity, Vector3, Vector3, float, float) Analytical two-bone IK (hip-knee-foot or shoulder-elbow-hand). Prefer this over FABRIK for limbs: it is exact, single-pass, and cannot oscillate. pole decides which side of the limb plane the knee (or elbow) bends to - typically a point in front of the character for legs, or off to the side for arms. Requires exactly three joints above and including entity and returns false otherwise; it will not silently fall back to a different solver. public static bool SetIKPositionTwoBone(Entity entity, Vector3 target, Vector3 pole, float weight = 1, float soften = 0) Parameters entity Entity target Vector3 pole Vector3 weight float Blend against the animated pose, 0..1. soften float Fraction of limb length over which reach eases out before the joint locks straight, 0..1. Softening always costs reach - at 1 a straight leg lands several centimetres short of the target - so it defaults to off and should only be dialled in to hide a snapping knee. Returns bool SetIKRotation(Entity, Quaternion, float) Blends entity toward a world-space orientation. Use after a position solve to orient a foot to the ground normal or to keep an aimed hand level. public static bool SetIKRotation(Entity entity, Quaternion rotation, float weight = 1) Parameters entity Entity rotation Quaternion weight float Returns bool

The document declares it with data-model="name" on an element; inside that element {{ credit }}, data-if, data-for, data-class-, data-style-, data-attr-, data-value, data-checked and data-event- read the model. public sealed class UIDataModel Inheritance object UIDataModel Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Examples // <body data-model="hud"> {{ credit | money }} <button data-event-click="Spin()"> var model = ui.GetModel("hud"); model.Bind(hud); // HudModel's public fields, properties, methods model.AddTransform<long>("money", v => $"{v:N0}"); hud.credit += win; model.Dirty(nameof(HudModel.credit)); Remarks Get it with GetModel(string); it exists before and across document (re)loads. Obtain instances via GetElementById(string) / QuerySelector(string); each element has one wrapper. A wrapper outliving its element (after an InnerRml rebuild of an ancestor, or a document close or reload) is safe: it reports IsValid() false, its setters do nothing and its getters return defaults. api/Unravel.Core.html.title: Namespace Unravel.Core | Unravel Engine Scripting API
api/Unravel.Core.html.summary: Namespace Unravel.Core Classes AnimationClip Animation clip asset handle. AnimationComponent Provides functionality to manage and blend animation clips on an entity. AnimationController Animation controller asset handle: a state machine of animation states, transitions and parameters. Assign it to controller and drive it with SetFloat(string, float), SetTrigger(string) and friends. Application Provides application-level functionality and control. Asset<T> Represents a generic asset with a unique identifier (UID). Assets Loads and resolves assets by key or unique identifier. Audio Global audio mixer controls (master + per-bus gains), fire-and-forget sounds and voice-limit info. AudioClip Audio clip asset handle. AudioListenerComponent Marks an entity as the audio listener used for spatialized sound. AudioSourceComponent Represents an audio source component that can play, pause, and control audio playback in a scene. AutoStaticsCleanupAttribute Marks a class whose static state must be reset when a script domain is unloaded (CoreCLR backend). On Mono, unloading a domain destroys its statics wholesale. On CoreCLR a collectible AssemblyLoadContext only unloads once nothing references it anymore, so static caches in a surviving assembly (e.g. managers holding script instances or script Type objects) would silently keep the unloaded domain alive. The runtime processes this attribute right before any domain is unloaded: If the class defines static void OnStaticsCleanup() (any visibility), that method is invoked and nothing else happens - use it to re-create managers or clear collections selectively. Otherwise every non-readonly static field is reset to its default value. Readonly statics cannot be cleared by reflection and produce a warning - define OnStaticsCleanup for those. The attribute is matched by name, so any assembly may use it without referencing the engine. On Mono it is ignored. BoneComponent Identifies a bone node in a skinned model armature. CameraComponent Camera component for viewport projection and screen-space queries. ChainIKComponent Iterative IK over any number of bones ending at the bone it sits on (tails, tentacles, spines, robot arms). CharacterControllerComponent Provides character controller physics functionality for an entity. Uses a capsule shape internally with sweep-based movement. Collision Represents a collision that occurs between two entities. Component Represents a base class for all components in the entity-component system. Coroutine A coroutine started with StartCoroutine(IEnumerator). Yield it from another coroutine to wait until it finishes. Cursor The mouse cursor: lock it for mouse look, keep it inside the game view, or hide it. EntityPool Reuses prefab instances via SetActive instead of Instantiate/Destroy each time. Suitable for high-churn gameplay objects (enemies, projectiles, pickups, VFX). ExceptionHelper Helpers for throwing managed exceptions from native bridge code. Font Font asset handle. FootIKComponent Plants a character feet on uneven ground: probes the ground under each foot, lowers the pelvis to the lowest planted foot, solves each leg with two-bone IK and tilts the feet onto the slope. Sits on the character root; the probes need physics, so it acts in play mode. GCMonitor Tracks managed GC activity and optionally logs collection/memory deltas. Gizmos Draws debug primitives in the scene for visualization during development. HeaderAttribute Adds a header to a field, providing a brief description or hint. HideAttribute Hides a field from the inspector, preventing it from being displayed or edited. IK Inverse-kinematics helpers for skeletal chains. Call these from OnUpdate. Scripts run after the animation system has evaluated the pose and before skinning, so bone writes made there are what gets rendered. Writing bones from OnFixedUpdate does not work - animation will overwrite them later in the frame. Every method returns true when a pose was written. A false means the chain was too short, the goal was not finite, or the weight was zero - not that the target was out of reach (an unreachable target still produces a valid stretched pose). The position solvers only orient the bones that drive the chain, never the end effector itself, so a solved foot keeps the orientation animation gave it. Follow a position solve with SetIKRotation(Entity, Quaternion, float) to pin a foot to a slope or keep an aimed hand level. Poles must come from a reference the solve does not move - the character root, or a dedicated hint entity. markdown/animation-retargeting.html.summary: Animation retargeting Retargeting plays a clip made for one skeleton on another: a clip from an animation pack on your own character, a clip exported from another tool, a clip of a taller or shorter rig. This page follows a clip from import to the pose on screen, then lists what to check when something looks wrong. It is written for people working in the editor and for agents driving the editor over MCP; the last section maps the code for engine work. Quick start Import the character model and the animation files (FBX or glTF). Animation-only files (a clip saved without its mesh) import too. Select the character entity. Its Animation component plays the clips. Pick Pose Retargeting: Copy (default) when the clips were exported with this model, or for this exact skeleton. Rest Aligned for anything else: another rig, other bone names, other units, other axes, other proportions. Leave Retargeting Mode on Name Based. Open Retarget Check in the Animation inspector. It shows how the clip playing (or one you pick) binds to this skeleton: channels matched and how, bones left unreached, the height ratio, the bone root motion moves, how far the two rest poses differ, and a warning for each problem it finds. Humanoid Mapping above it lists the bone found for each role; its pencil button sets a role by hand when the wrong bone was found. When the clip's skeleton and the character rest in different poses (an A-pose clip on a T-pose character), set Retarget Pose to T-Pose: both skeletons are straightened before motion is carried over. When a character of other proportions puts its limbs through its body (short arms beside a big head and a wide body), add Retarget Pose Offsets: raising both upper arms 20 to 30 degrees keeps them clear in every clip. For clips that travel (walks, rolls, attacks that lunge), turn on Apply Root Motion and check each clip's root motion import settings. Concepts Rest pose. The pose a skeleton is built in, before any animation: usually a T-pose or an A-pose. Retarget pose. The pose Rest Aligned retargeting measures motion from on the clip's skeleton and applies it to on the character. By default each skeleton's rest pose, so both must rest in the same physical pose; with Retarget Pose T-Pose, both rests straightened to a T-pose; on the character, turned further by its Retarget Pose Offsets. Channel. One animated node of a clip: its name and its position, rotation and scale keys, in the node's local space (relative to its parent). Humanoid roles. Twenty-two bones every humanoid has in some form: hips, spine, chest, upper chest, neck, head, and per side shoulder, upper arm, lower arm, hand, upper leg, lower leg, foot and toes. The engine finds them from the skeleton's shape (two legs hang from the hips, the spine rises to where the arms branch, and so on), not from a table of names. Names only tell left from right; side-less names take their side from the way the toes point. Twist joints (lShldrTwist) and split segments (upper_arm.L.001) are passed over. 1. Import: what a clip records Each animation in a model file becomes its own .anim asset named <file>_<animation>. A clip holds: Channels, one per animated node. The source rest pose. For each channel: the node's rest transform in the file, the channel that animates its nearest animated ancestor, and the fixed transform of any unanimated nodes in between. The clip carries a description of the skeleton it was made on, so the character it was authored for never has to be imported. Root-motion nodes. The importer picks the shallowest animated node on the skeleton's trunk (from the scene root down to where the skeleton branches): a root bone when the rig has one, else the hips. Its travel and turn can move the entity instead of the bone. Import settings (in the clip's .meta, edited in the clip inspector): root motion options, plus the events and curves authored on the clip's timeline. Import setting Default Effect Keep Position Y on Vertical motion stays in the pose (a jump lifts the hips, not the entity). Keep Position XZ off Horizontal travel stays in the pose instead of moving the entity. Keep Rotation off Turns stay in the pose instead of turning the entity. Keep In Place off Travel is removed: the clip plays on the spot and moves nothing. Files without meshes take every animated node and its ancestors as their skeleton, and an FBX root gets the same axis correction a file with meshes gets, so a clip-only export describes the same skeleton as the skinned one. 2. Setup: the Animation component Setting Values Meaning Retargeting Mode Name Based (default), Index Based How channels find bones. Name Based matches bone names; Index Based uses the node order in the file and only suits clips from the same file. Pose Retargeting Copy (default), Rest Aligned How a pose reaches the bones. Copy writes the clip's local transforms as they are; Rest Aligned maps the motion from the clip's skeleton onto this one. Rest Aligned needs Name Based. Retarget Pose Bind Pose (default), T-Pose Rest Aligned only. Bind Pose measures motion from each skeleton's rest pose. T-Pose first straightens both skeletons by role: upper and lower arms level along the character's sides, upper and lower legs straight down. Copies of one skeleton play the same either way. Retarget Pose Offsets role + rotation (degrees) Rest Aligned only. Turns of this character's bones in its retarget pose, in its own space: about its side axis (towards its left), up and forward. Right-side roles are mirrored, so (0, 0, 20) on both upper arms raises both. Every clip keeps them. Apply Root Motion off / on Moves the entity by the clip's root motion. With a Character Controller in play mode the move goes through it, so it collides. Copy is exact and fast when the skeletons really are the same. Across different skeletons it is wrong in visible ways: positions copy the source's bone lengths (limbs stretch or shrink), and rotations assume the same bone axes (a rig whose bones point along +Y twists on one whose bones point along +X). The target side of Rest Aligned is built from the model: its bone names, parents and bind pose, and the humanoid roles found in that bind pose. Roles set by hand. Where the finder picks the wrong bone (a rig that animates a hand bone below the wrist it found), set the role in the model file's import settings: Rig > Humanoid Overrides, a role and a bone name each, an empty name taking the role away. The pencil button in Humanoid Mapping writes them for you. They are compiled into the model and into every clip of the file, so they hold where the skeleton plays clips and where its clips play on others. The model is imported again when they change. 3. Binding: done once per clip and skeleton The first time a clip plays on a character, the player binds the clip to the skeleton and keeps the result until the clip or the model's armature changes. Channels find bones, first match wins: the same name; the same name without its FBX namespace (mixamorig:Hips and mixamorig1:Hips); Rest Aligned only: the same humanoid role. The clip's skeleton gets its roles from its recorded rest pose, so upperarm_l, mixamorig:LeftArm and DEF-upper_arm.L all land on the target's left upper arm. Roles set by hand win on both sides. Bones no channel reaches keep their bind pose. Retarget poses. Each skeleton's rest pose, straightened to a T-pose when Retarget Pose asks for it; the character's then turned by its offsets. Frame fit. The two skeletons may stand in different frames: a Z-up export against a Y-up one, or a model the importer turned to face forward. The rotation that best lays the source joint positions onto the target's (in the retarget poses, without the offsets) is that frame difference. Joint positions do not depend on how a rig orients its bone axes, so the fit captures the frame only. Two humanoids both stand upright, so between them only the fit's heading (its turn about the up axis) is kept: where their proportions differ (a leaning spine, a big head) the fit tilts, and every carried motion would lean with it. Height ratio. The target's hip height over the source's. A shorter character takes shorter steps and jumps lower. Root-motion target. The root channel is matched like any other. When the target lacks that bone (a clip with a floor-level root bone on a rig that starts at the hips), the motion reports through the root's first matched descendant, normally the hips. 4. Each frame: posing the target Copy writes each channel's sampled local transform onto its bone. Rest Aligned samples the whole source pose, unmatched channels included (a root the target lacks still carries its children), builds it up to world space, and then poses each matched bone: Rotation. How far the source bone turned from its retarget pose, in world space, is carried into the target's frame by the frame fit and applied on top of the target bone's retarget pose. Each rig keeps its own bone axes; only the change is carried. Position. The target keeps its bone lengths. Only the source bone's move away from its rest (the hips bobbing, say) is carried, turned into the target's frame and scaled by the height ratio. Scale. A change of scale is carried along the same physical direction: a stretch along a source bone that points along +Y stretches a target bone that points along +X along its length. Layers, crossfades, blend spaces and animation controllers all sample through the same binding. A blend space whose clips share one source skeleton is blended in that skeleton and retargeted once, which gives the pose retargeting each clip separately would, for less work. 5. Root motion The root's move over the frame is measured in its parent's frame on the source skeleton. It is carried into the target root's parent frame with the heading of the frame fit only (so the character never tilts), scaled by the height ratio, then mapped through the target's bones to the entity, which moves once per frame. The first frame of a clip moves the entity too, so travel does not depend on the frame rate. During a crossfade the moves of both clips blend by the crossfade weight. Troubleshooting Start with the Animation inspector's Retarget Check (MCP: animation_get_retarget): its warnings name most of the causes below. Symptom Likely cause Fix Character lies down, twists or stretches Copy with clips from another export or rig Set Pose Retargeting to Rest Aligned. Nothing moves Index Based with clips from another file, or no names or roles match Use Name Based; check Humanoid Mapping on both sides. Arms held too high or too low through every clip The rest poses differ (T-pose against A-pose); Retarget Check's Rest poses list shows the angle per limb Set Retarget Pose to T-Pose. Limbs pass through the body or the head The character's proportions differ (short arms, wide body, big head): human angles land inside it Add Retarget Pose Offsets, for example raise both upper arms 20 to 30 degrees. A limb or a hand does not move, or moves the wrong bone The finder gave the role to another bone (a hand role on the wrist while the clips animate the hand) Set the role by hand: the pencil button in Humanoid Mapping, or the model file's Rig > Humanoid Overrides. Fingers, tail or accessory bones stay still They match neither by name nor by role (roles cover 22 body bones) Give them the same names on both rigs; FBX namespaces are already ignored. Left and right swapped Side-less bone names read the wrong way Check Humanoid Mapping; name the sides (_l, .R, Left). Steps too long or too short, feet slide Proportions differ; the hips found on one side are wrong Check that both sides found their hips; add Foot IK for contact. Character walks away from its entity and snaps back at the loop Root motion is not applied Turn on Apply Root Motion; check the clip's Keep Position XZ. Character drifts upward or sinks Vertical root motion moves the entity Keep Position Y on (the default). For agents (MCP) Set up a character for clips from other rigs: {"name": "scene_set_component_properties_batch", "arguments": {"items": [ {"entity_id": "<character>", "component": "Animation", "properties": {"retargeting_mode": "name_based", "pose_retargeting": "rest_aligned", "apply_root_motion": true}}]}} Check how a clip binds to the character. Without clip it checks the clip the base layer plays, else the one its controller starts in, else the Animation clip; "channels": true lists every channel with its bone and kind of match: {"name": "animation_get_retarget", "arguments": {"entity_id": "<character>", "clip": "app:/data/Characters/Pack/Pack_Walk.anim"}} It returns the mode in effect, match counts per kind, the unmatched channels, the unreached bones, height_ratio, the frame turn, the root-motion channel and bone, rest differences per limb in degrees, and warnings; an empty warnings list is the goal. Straighten both skeletons, raise a stocky character's arms, and set a role by hand (the model file is imported again): {"name": "scene_set_component_properties_batch", "arguments": {"items": [ {"entity_id": "<character>", "component": "Animation", "properties": {"retarget_pose": "t_pose", "retarget_pose_offsets": [ {"role": "left_upper_arm", "rotation": [0, 0, 25]}, {"role": "right_upper_arm", "rotation": [0, 0, 25]}]}}]}} {"name": "assets_set_import_settings", "arguments": {"wait_ms": 120000, "items": [ {"key": "app:/data/Characters/Pack/Pack.glb", "settings": {"rig": {"humanoid_overrides": [ {"role": "left_hand", "bone": "hand.l"}, {"role": "right_hand", "bone": "hand.r"}]}}}]}} Check the roles on both sides; every role the clip uses should exist on the character (overrides lists the roles set by hand): {"name": "animation_get_humanoid", "arguments": {"entity_id": "<character>"}} {"name": "animation_get_humanoid", "arguments": {"clip": "app:/data/Characters/Pack/Pack_Walk.anim"}} Read and change a clip's root motion settings (the clip is imported again with them): {"name": "assets_get_import_settings", "arguments": {"keys": ["app:/data/Characters/Pack/Pack_Walk.anim"]}} {"name": "assets_set_import_settings", "arguments": {"items": [ {"key": "app:/data/Characters/Pack/Pack_Walk.anim", "settings": {"root_motion": {"keep_position_xz": false}}}]}} Verify on screen, not from reads alone: enter play mode, pause, step with play_skip_frame and capture with viewport_capture_scene; animation_get_state reports the clips and weights playing. Compare a retargeted crouch, sit or landing against the floor, and the hips' height standing still against the character's proportions.
